info.title: rypt
info.description:
Multi-tenant encryption as a service in front of Google Cloud KMS. A
tenant authenticates with an API token and never touches GCP: key material
lives in one GCP project owned by the operator.

Two modes are offered. **Direct** — `encrypt` and `decrypt` of payloads up
to 64 KiB. **Envelope** — `wrap`, `unwrap` and `rewrap` of data keys.

Binary fields are standard base64 with padding, on the way in and on the
way out. Every response carries an `x-request-id` header, and every error
body repeats it.

Two credentials reach this API. An **API token** (`bearerAuth`) is the
machine credential and is the only one the five metered cryptographic
operations accept. An **Auth0 access token** (`consoleAuth`) is what the
dashboard uses, and is the only one that may mint or revoke an API token.
Both resolve to one tenant, and the endpoints in between — the key
lifecycle, usage and the audit log — take either. The console endpoints
exist only where a deployment has configured Auth0; without it they are not
routes.

Four tiers decide the Cloud KMS protection level, how many key versions
are retained, how many operations a month are included, and what one
past that costs. A key's tier is fixed at creation. A rotation retires
the versions beyond the retained count, and each keeps decrypting for
seven days before it is destroyed.

| tier | protection | retained versions | ops included per month | past the cap | per key-month | per op past the cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `free` | wrapped | 1 | 10,000 | `encrypt`, `wrap`, `rewrap` refused, `429 ops_cap_reached`; `decrypt`, `unwrap` go on | — | — |
| `wrapped` | wrapped | 1 | 50,000 | recorded as overage | $3.00 | $0.00001 |
| `software` | SOFTWARE | 3 | 100,000 | recorded as overage | $10.00 | $0.00002 |
| `hsm` | HSM | 2 | 250,000 | recorded as overage | $35.00 | $0.00005 |

`wrapped` is the free tier's backend without its hard cap: a rypt data key
wrapped by a shared Cloud KMS root, so it costs no CryptoKey of its own.
Prices are before tax, and a paid key is billed in arrears, by the UTC
calendar month.

From October 2026 each paid key is billed by the day. Its monthly fee, the
price of a key-month, is split evenly across the days of the month, and
the key pays for every day it exists in, even part of a day: one that
exists all month pays the whole fee, and one made and deleted the same day
pays one day. Its included operations are split the same way, rounded down
— a key that exists for 10 days of a 30-day month includes 10/30 of its
tier's ops included per month — and every operation past that share is
overage, at the price in the last column.

Deleting a key stops its billing after the day its deletion is requested,
not when it is destroyed. Restoring a key is free as an action, but the
key is then billed as if it was never deleted: its pending days are
billed. A month that has already ended is not reopened, though: pending
days in an earlier month stay unbilled, and that month's included
operations stay as they were at its end.

A month before October 2026 is billed by the key-month: a paid key pays a
whole key-month, and gets the whole allowance, for every month it exists in
at any point, with three exceptions. A paid key deleted within 24 hours of
being created, and not restored, is never billed a key-month; a key's
billing ends when its deletion is requested, not when it is destroyed; and
a key created on a month's last day (UTC) is not billed for that month.

Deleting a key does not destroy it. The key is pending deletion for seven
days: it refuses every operation with `409 key_pending_deletion`, keeps
its name and its versions, and can be restored, which is free as an action
and bills the key as above. It is destroyed after that, or at once with
delete now from the console.

Keys, API tokens and firewalls live in **containers**, and an API token
never sees outside its own: another container's key is the same `404` as
another tenant's, everywhere, and it creates keys in its own container
alone. Every tenant has a default container, which everything goes in unless
told otherwise; the console makes, renames and deletes the rest. A console
session sees every container.

Within its container an API token can be restricted from the console: held
to a **firewall**, a named list of networks that any number of the
container's API tokens can share, and to particular keys. One used from
outside its firewall's networks is `403 ip_not_allowed`, checked before
its secret and before its rate limit, so a request the firewall refuses
never spends the key's 100 requests a second. One restricted to
particular keys is
`403 key_not_allowed` on any other key, cannot create a key, and sees only
its own keys in `GET /v1/keys` and `GET /v1/usage`. A change to either, a
firewall's networks included, applies from the key's next request.

An API token may also do only what it was given: its `allowed_actions`. Six
use or rotate the keys it may act on — `encrypt`, `decrypt`, `wrap`,
`unwrap`, `rewrap` and `rotate` — and four manage them: `create`, `rename`,
`delete` and `restore`. Anything else on those routes is
`403 action_not_allowed`, and is recorded in the audit log as that
operation, failed. A new key is given nothing unless its creator names
something, and API tokens made before 0.8.0 have at most the first six, so
they cannot create, rename, delete or restore a key until they are given
those actions. The decision is made by a Cerbos policy decision point
running beside the service; when it does not answer, the request is
`503 unavailable`, never allowed. A key that is not one of the API token's
container's live keys is a `404` before anything is asked, whatever the
action, and the policy decision point is told the tenant and container
of the API token and of the key and allows nothing across either, as a
second check beside the service's own.

An eleventh action, `read`, is needed from 0.14.0 to list keys
(`GET /v1/keys`), read a key (`GET /v1/keys/{id}`) and its audit log,
and read usage (`GET /v1/usage`); without it they are
`403 action_not_allowed`, which is not recorded in the audit log, as no
read is. Every API token that existed when 0.14.0 was deployed was given
`read` then; one made afterwards has it only if it is given it. Reads
now ask the policy decision point too, so when it does not answer they
are `503 unavailable` like everything else an API token does.

Billing is the deployment's choice. Where it is configured (which needs
the console too), a tenant may hold one live `free` key — a free key
pending deletion still holds the place — a paid key can
only be created while the tenant's billing is in good standing, and
`encrypt`, `wrap` and `rewrap` on a paid key are refused with
`402 billing_required` once it is not — while `decrypt` and `unwrap`
keep working, so lapsed billing never holds data hostage. Where it is
not configured, none of that applies and every tier is open to every
tenant.

tags.name: keys
tags.description:
Key lifecycle — create, list, read, rename, rotate, and deletion:
delete, restore and destroy.

tags.name: audit
tags.description: The append-only record of every mutating operation.

tags.name: usage
tags.description: Per-key operation counters for a calendar month.

tags.name: console
tags.description:
The dashboard API: the signed-in user, the containers, the API tokens they
issue and restrict, the firewalls they hold them to, and the tenant's
billing. Auth0 access tokens only — an API token may not
mint or revoke a credential, or spend the tenant's money. Present only
when the deployment configures a console; the billing endpoints only
when it configures billing too.

tags.name: billing
tags.description:
Stripe's side of billing: the webhook Stripe delivers subscription
events to. Not for clients. Present only when the deployment
configures billing.

post.description:
Creates a Cloud KMS CryptoKey (or, for a `free` or `wrapped` key while
a wrapped root is configured, a wrapped key in Postgres) and returns
the `key` object. The name must be unique among the tenant's live keys,
which include keys pending deletion; a collision is `409 key_exists`. A
key's name is free again once the key is destroyed.

Where the deployment configures billing, two more rules apply. A
tenant holds at most one live `free` key, so a second is
`409 free_key_exists`; a free key pending deletion still counts, and
destroying it frees the slot. And a paid
tier — `wrapped`, `software` or `hsm` — needs the tenant's billing in
good standing, because the key starts accruing a monthly fee the
moment it exists: without it the request is `402 billing_required`,
and the refusal is audited as a failed `create_key`.

The key goes in `container_id`: for an API token its own container,
which is also where it goes when the field is absent, and naming any
other is `400 invalid_container`; for a console session any of the
tenant's containers, or the default one when absent. Its name is unique
among its container's live keys.

An API token restricted to particular keys is `403 key_not_allowed`,
audited the same way: the key it made would be outside its own list.
Then an API token needs `create` among its `allowed_actions`: without it
the request is `403 action_not_allowed`, also audited as a failed
`create_key`. A console session needs neither.

name.description:
1–128 characters, no control characters, unique among the
tenant's live keys, pending ones included. A name that is
only whitespace is also rejected, which this schema cannot
express.

container_id.description:
The container the key goes in, fixed at creation. Absent:
an API token's own container, or the tenant's default for a
console session.

409.description:
`key_exists` — the tenant already has a live key with that name,
pending deletion or not — or, where billing is configured,
`free_key_exists`: the tier is `free` and the tenant already has a
live `free` key, pending deletion or not.

get.description:
The live keys the caller may see, oldest first: every key not yet
destroyed, those pending deletion included — for a console session the
whole tenant's, for an API token its container's, and for one restricted
to particular keys only those. Not metered, not audited.

A key pending deletion is returned like any other, with its `state`;
a destroyed key is `404`. Not metered, not audited.

patch.description:
Gives the key a new name and returns it. The name is the only thing
about a key that changes after it is created: its id, tier, versions
and ciphertext are untouched, so nothing that uses the key by its id
notices. The new name is held to the rules of a name at creation and
must be unique among the tenant's live keys, pending ones included;
a collision is `409 key_exists`. The old name is free at once.

A key pending deletion is `409 key_pending_deletion` and keeps its name
until it is restored. Renaming a key to the name it already has changes
nothing, answers the same `200` and writes no audit row; every other
attempt, refused or not, is audited as `rename_key`. An API token needs
`rename` among its `allowed_actions`: without it the request is
`403 action_not_allowed`, audited as a failed `rename_key`.

name.description:
1–128 characters, no control characters, unique among the
tenant's live keys, pending ones included. A name that is
only whitespace is also rejected, which this schema cannot
express.

409.description:
`key_exists` — another live key of the tenant's, pending deletion
or not, has that name — or `key_pending_deletion`: this key is
pending deletion and refuses every operation until it is restored.

delete.description:
Puts the key in pending deletion and returns it. Nothing is destroyed
and Cloud KMS is not called: from now on every operation on the key —
the five cryptographic ones, `decrypt` and `unwrap` included, and
`rotate` — is `409 key_pending_deletion`, while the key keeps its name
and its versions. It is destroyed after `destroy_after`, seven days
on, unless it is restored first with `POST /v1/keys/{id}/restore`.
`POST /v1/keys/{id}/destroy`, from the console, destroys it at once.

Deleting a key that is already pending changes nothing, its dates
included, and answers the same, so a retried request is harmless; only
the first is audited. An API token needs `delete` among its
`allowed_actions`: without it the request is `403 action_not_allowed`,
audited as a failed `delete_key`.

Deleting a paid key stops its billing after the day of the request,
not when the key is destroyed. From October 2026 a key is billed by
the day, that day included. Restoring it is free as an action, but the
key is then billed as if it was never deleted: its pending days are
billed, except those in a month that has already ended, which is not
reopened. In a month before October 2026 its key-months stop with the
month of the request, and a paid key deleted within 24 hours of being
created, and not restored, is never billed a key-month.

post.description:
Creates a new version and makes it primary, so new ciphertext is made
under it. The versions beyond the tier's retained count (`free` 1,
`wrapped` 1, `software` 3, `hsm` 2), oldest first, are retired: each
keeps decrypting, unwrapping and rewrapping for seven days, and is
listed in `retiring_versions` with the time it is destroyed. A version
already retiring does not count against the retained count, and keeps
its date.

On `free` and `wrapped` there is exactly one retained version, so every
rotation retires the previous one. **Rotate, then rewrap within seven
days** everything still under the retired version: once it is
destroyed, that ciphertext can never be decrypted again, and
`decrypt`, `unwrap` and `rewrap` answer `400 invalid_ciphertext`.

A key may have at most ten versions retiring at once. A rotation that
would go past that is `409 too_many_retiring_versions`, and creates
nothing; the message says when the next one is destroyed. A key
pending deletion is `409 key_pending_deletion`. Where billing is
configured, a paid key whose tenant's billing has lapsed is `402
billing_required`: rewrap is refused then, so a rotation would leave
data that could be read but never moved off the retired version. For
the same reason a `free` key at its monthly cap is `429
ops_cap_reached` until the cap resets. Takes no request body.

200.description: The key, with its new primary version.

409.description:
`key_pending_deletion` — the key is pending deletion and refuses
every operation until it is restored — or
`too_many_retiring_versions`: the key already has ten versions
retiring, and the message says when the next one is destroyed.

post.description:
Takes the key out of pending deletion and returns it active again.
Restoring is free as an action, but the key is then billed as if it
was never deleted: its pending days are billed. A month that has
already ended is not reopened: pending days in an earlier month stay
unbilled, and that month's included operations stay as they were at
its end.

Once `destroy_after` has passed the key can no longer be restored,
even while it is still listed as pending: its destruction may already
have begun.

An API token needs `restore` among its `allowed_actions`: without it the
request is `403 action_not_allowed`, audited as a failed `restore_key`.

Takes no request body.

409.description:
`not_pending_deletion` — the key is not pending deletion, so there
is nothing to restore — or `restore_window_closed`: its
`destroy_after` has passed and it is being destroyed.

post.description:
Delete now: schedules every enabled version for destruction and
destroys the key at once, whether it was pending deletion or not —
for a key that must stop existing now rather than in seven days. From
then on it is `404` like an id that was never issued, and its name,
and a free key's place, are free immediately. This cannot be undone
from the API or the dashboard; Cloud KMS keeps the key material for its
own 24-hour destruction window, which only the operator can reach
into.

The key is first made pending and due, and only then destroyed. If
the destruction fails part-way it stays that way: it refuses every
operation, answers restore with `409 restore_window_closed`, and is
destroyed by a retry or, within minutes while the service is busy, by
the service itself.

Console only, like minting an API token: an API token that leaked can
delete keys, but each such deletion waits seven days and can be
undone, whereas one that could destroy would take them for good. An
API token is `403 session_required`.

A key destroyed while pending keeps the time its deletion was
requested, and its billing still ends then, not when it is destroyed:
from October 2026 it is billed through the day of the request, and in
a month before, one deleted within 24 hours of being created is still
not billed. Takes no request body.

One metered operation. The ciphertext names the key version it was made
under, so `decrypt` keeps working across rotations with no metadata
stored by the caller.

On the `hsm` tier `plaintext` and `aad` may total at most 8,176 bytes
decoded — Cloud KMS's own 8,192-byte HSM limit, less the 16 bytes of
tenant id the service binds into the AAD — tighter than the limit each
field carries here. That combined rule is per-tier and cannot be
expressed in this schema.

On a paid key, where the deployment configures billing, this is
`402 billing_required` while the tenant's billing is not in good
standing: new ciphertext is what a paid key is for. It is refused
before Cloud KMS is called, audited, and not counted.

plaintext.description:
Payload to encrypt, standard padded base64. 1–65,536 bytes
decoded; empty is rejected.

aad.description:
Additional authenticated data, standard padded base64, at
most 65,520 bytes decoded on a `software` or `hsm` key and
65,536 on a `free` or `wrapped` one. The service binds the
tenant id into it, so the ciphertext opens only for this
tenant. The same value must be presented on `decrypt` and
`rewrap`. Omit it, send `null`, or send `""`, when none
was used.

post.description:
One metered operation. Works for any version the key still retains, not
just the primary.

A ciphertext the backend refuses, an `aad` that does not match, or a
ciphertext naming a version that is no longer enabled is
`400 invalid_ciphertext`.

Never refused for billing: a tenant whose billing has lapsed can
still read back everything it encrypted. Refused, like every
operation, on a key pending deletion: restore the key to use it.

ciphertext.description: A ciphertext this key produced, standard padded base64.

aad.description:
The same additional authenticated data the ciphertext was
made with. Omit it, send `null`, or send `""`, when none
was used.

post.description:
One metered operation. With no `dek`, rypt generates 32 random bytes
and returns both the data key and its wrapped form; with a `dek` of 16,
24 or 32 bytes, only `wrapped` comes back.

An optional `aad` binds the wrapped key to its context, so a `wrapped`
value copied to another record does not unwrap there: `unwrap` must be
given the same `aad`, and a mismatch is `400 invalid_ciphertext`.

Send `{}` to have one generated.

On a paid key, where the deployment configures billing, this is
`402 billing_required` while the tenant's billing is not in good
standing, as `encrypt` is. It is refused before Cloud KMS is called,
audited, and not counted.

dek.description:
Data key to wrap, standard padded base64, decoding to 16,
24 or 32 bytes. Absent or `null` means "generate one", and
then the response returns it.

aad.description:
Additional authenticated data, standard padded base64, at
most 65,520 bytes decoded on a `software` or `hsm` key and
65,536 on a `free` or `wrapped` one, binding the wrapped
key to its context. The same value must be presented on
`unwrap`. On an `hsm` key, `dek` and `aad` may total at
most 8,176 bytes. Omit it, send `null`, or send `""`, for
none.

200.description:
The wrapped data key, and the data key itself if rypt
generated it.

dek.description:
The generated data key, base64 — present only when the
request supplied no `dek`. A caller that sent one already
has it, so the field is absent from the body entirely
rather than null.

wrapped.description:
The wrapped data key, base64, to be stored next to the
payload it protects and handed back to `unwrap`.

post.description:
One metered operation.

Never refused for billing: a tenant whose billing has lapsed can
still unwrap every data key it wrapped. Refused, like every operation,
on a key pending deletion: restore the key to use it.

aad.description:
The same additional authenticated data the data key was
wrapped with, standard padded base64. Omit it, send `null`,
or send `""`, when none was used.

post.summary: Re-encrypt a ciphertext under the current primary version
post.description:
Decrypts under whatever version the ciphertext names and re-encrypts
under the current primary, without the plaintext leaving the process.
One metered operation despite the two KMS calls.

On a paid key, where the deployment configures billing, this is
`402 billing_required` while the tenant's billing is not in good
standing, as `encrypt` is: it produces new ciphertext. A tenant in
that state can still `decrypt` what it has.

ciphertext.description:
A ciphertext this key produced, standard padded
base64.

aad.description:
The same additional authenticated data the ciphertext was
made with; it is reapplied to the new ciphertext. Omit it,
send `null`, or send `""`, when none was used.

get.description:
Events newest first, for a key the tenant owns, keys pending deletion
and destroyed keys included.
Not metered, not audited: looking at the log must not grow it.

Every operation that changes the key or uses its material is an event,
successful or not. That includes an API token refused one of them: an
action it was not given is the operation with `result` `error` and
`error_code` `action_not_allowed`, and a key outside its `key_ids` is
the same with `key_not_allowed`. Every refusal is its own event. A
refusal about a key that is not a live key of the API token's own
container records nothing, and neither does a firewall refusal or a
bad credential.

The window is half-open — `since` inclusive, `until` exclusive — and
`ts` is rendered to microseconds, so a returned `ts` round-trips
exactly as a bound. `since`/`until` select a window rather than acting
as a lossless cursor, so choose a `limit` that covers the window you
ask for.

A parameter that is present but empty is a value like any other and is
rejected; only an absent parameter takes its default.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description:
Oldest timestamp to include, RFC 3339 with an offset.
Inclusive.

parameters.name: until
parameters.description: Timestamp to stop before, RFC 3339 with an offset. Exclusive.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many events to return. Defaults to 100.

200.description: The key's audit events, newest first.

get.description:
One line per live key, pending deletion or not — zeros when it did
nothing — plus any destroyed key that performed operations in the
period. An API token sees its container's lines, and one restricted to
particular keys only theirs. Not metered, not audited: looking at the
report must not change it.

The window is the calendar month in UTC. A `period` that is present but
empty is rejected; only an absent `period` takes the default.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Month to report on. Defaults to the current UTC month.

get.summary: Read the signed-in user and the tenant they act as
get.description:
Who this console session belongs to, and which tenant every other
endpoint will scope it to. The first request from an Auth0 subject this
service has not seen provisions a user, a tenant and an owner
membership; every later one is a read.

`email` and `name` are what the access token carried. Auth0 puts neither
in an access token by default, so both are null unless an Action adds
them — a dashboard that wants a profile to display already has one, in
the ID token Auth0 gave the browser.

The Auth0 `sub` is deliberately not returned. `user.id` is the
identifier that appears in this API's own audit log.

200.description: The session's user, tenant and role.

post.description:
Mints an API token for the session's tenant and returns its token
**once**. The token is not stored and cannot be recovered: the database
holds only its Argon2id hash. Store it before leaving the response.

It lives in `container_id`, or the tenant's default container when
that is absent, for good: `400 invalid_container` for one that is not a
live container of the tenant's.

`allowed_actions` is what it may do with the keys of its container.
Absent is none, and none allows nothing. Its creation is appended to
the container's permission chain, and the response carries the chain's
new head. On `encrypt`, `decrypt`, `wrap`, `unwrap`, `rewrap` and
`rotate`, renaming, deleting and restoring a key, and creating one, an
action the key was not given is `403 action_not_allowed`. `create`
works only for a key with no `key_ids`.

An API token may not call this. A key that could issue its successor
would outlive its own revocation, so revoking a leaked one would no
longer contain it.

container_id.description:
The container it lives in and never sees outside of, or the
tenant's default when absent.

name.description:
Label for the key. Required: the listing carries no prefix,
so this is the only thing that distinguishes two of a
tenant's keys — and the endpoint you would reach for
without it is the one that revokes them. Not only
whitespace, which the pattern cannot express.

201.description: The new key, with its one-time token.

get.description:
Every key this tenant has, newest first, revoked ones included — a
revoked key that vanished would take with it the explanation for its own
audit trail.

Never the token, never the hash, and deliberately never the prefix: the
per-key rate limit is charged on the prefix lookup, before the Argon2
verification, so a prefix alone drains that key's budget. `name` is what
tells two keys apart, which is why it is required at creation.

patch.description:
Holds an API token to a firewall, to particular keys, or both, or lifts
either, sets what it may do with those keys, and returns the key. All
of these come from the key's own container. Each restriction has three
states: absent leaves that restriction as it is, `null` lifts it, and a
value replaces it. An empty key list is `400`: a key allowed on nothing
is a revoked key, and revoking says so. `allowed_actions` is absent or
a list, which may be empty; `null` is `400 invalid_allowed_actions`. An
unknown field is `400 invalid_request` rather than ignored, so a
misspelt one cannot leave a key unrestricted while answering 200.

A change to `key_ids` or `allowed_actions` is appended to the
container's permission chain in the same transaction, and the response
carries the chain's head after the request, moved or not. A change to
the firewall alone is not appended.

Either applies from the key's very next request, because it is read in
the same lookup that finds the key. A key used from outside its
firewall's networks is `403 ip_not_allowed`; one used on a key outside
`key_ids` is `403 key_not_allowed`, cannot create keys, and lists only
its own keys and their usage. A key named in `key_ids` and later
destroyed stays named and allows nothing, so a key never widens to its
whole container when its last one goes. A firewall refusal is logged,
not audited. A `key_not_allowed` refusal of an operation the audit log
records, and an `action_not_allowed` one, is audited as that operation
with `result` `error`: for a create always, and otherwise when the key
is a live key of the API token's own container.

Console only: a key that could lift its own restrictions would not be
restricted by them. A revoked key, another tenant's, and an id never
issued are the same 404, unaudited. Every other request that changes
something, or is refused, is audited as `update_api_token`; one that
changes nothing answers the same 200 and writes no row.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The API token's id, as `GET /v1/api-tokens` reports it.

firewall_id.description:
A live firewall of the key's container; another
container's, a deleted one and an unknown id are
`400 invalid_firewall`. `null` holds it to none.

key_ids.description:
Keys of the API token's container it may act on, each a live
one; one pending deletion counts, a destroyed one does not,
and another container's is `400 invalid_key_ids`. Repeats
are dropped, and the list is stored sorted. `null` allows
every key of its container.

200.description:
The API token, restricted as it now is, and the head of its
container's permission chain.

delete.description:
Revocation takes effect on the very next request the key makes: the
prefix lookup runs every time, so nothing is cached that could keep a
revoked key working.

Idempotent — a key that was already revoked is still 204, because the
state the caller asked for is the state that holds. A key belonging to
another tenant and an id that was never issued are the same 404.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The API token's id, as `GET /v1/api-tokens` reports it.

get.description:
The tenant's live containers, the default first and the rest oldest
first. Not audited.

post.description:
Makes an empty container. Its name has a key name's rules and is
unique among the tenant's live containers: `409 container_exists`
otherwise. Every attempt is audited as `create_container`.

name.description: Unique among the tenant's live containers.

409.description: `container_exists`: the tenant has a live container with that name.

patch.description:
Renames a container, the default included. A name another live
container holds is `409 container_exists`. Renaming to the name it has
changes nothing, answers the same and writes no audit row; every other
attempt is audited as `rename_container`. Another tenant's container,
a deleted one and an id never issued are the same 404, unaudited.

name.description: Unique among the tenant's live containers.

409.description:
`container_exists`: the tenant has another live container with that
name.

delete.description:
Deletes an empty container that is not the default. Nothing that
lives in it may remain: a key, one pending deletion included, a live
API token, or a firewall. A destroyed key and a revoked API token do not
count. Its name is free again at once. Refusals are audited as
`delete_container`; another tenant's container, a deleted one and an
id never issued are the same 404, unaudited.

409.description:
`container_is_default`: the default container cannot be deleted; or
`container_not_empty`: it still holds keys, live API tokens or
firewalls, which the message counts.

get.summary: Read the head of a container's permission chain
get.description:
Every change to what a container's API tokens may do is appended to the
container's permission chain, each entry naming the SHA-256 hash of the
one before it. The latest entry's hash, the head, stands for the whole
history: kept somewhere this service cannot reach, it is what a
rewritten history would fail to match.

The first read of a container's head may start its chain, which writes
its first entries; every later read only reads. Another tenant's
container, a deleted one and an id never issued are the same 404.

The tenant's live firewalls, every container's, oldest first. Each
names its container. Not audited.

post.description:
Makes a firewall in `container_id`, or the tenant's default container
when absent: `400 invalid_container` for one that is not a live
container of the tenant's. Its name has a key name's rules and is
unique among its container's firewalls (`409 firewall_exists`). Hold
API tokens of that container to it with `PATCH /v1/api-tokens/{id}`.
Every attempt is audited as `create_firewall`.

container_id.description: The container it goes in; the default when absent.

name.description: Unique among its container's live firewalls.

allowed_ips.description:
Networks a request presenting one of its API tokens may come
from: an address, which allows that address alone, or a
network in CIDR notation. `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` allow a
whole address family. Refused with `400
invalid_allowed_ips`: a network with bits set past its
prefix (`203.0.113.5/24`), an IPv4 address written as IPv6
(`::ffff:203.0.113.5`), and surrounding whitespace. Repeats
are dropped, and the list is stored sorted.

409.description: `firewall_exists`: its container has a live firewall with that name.

patch.description:
Renames a firewall, replaces its networks, or both; a field left out
stays as it was, and an unknown one is `400 invalid_request`. New
networks apply to every API token held to it from their next request. A
change that changes nothing answers the same and writes no audit row;
every other attempt is audited as `update_firewall`. Another tenant's
firewall, a deleted one and an id never issued are the same 404,
unaudited.

name.description: Unique among its container's live firewalls.

allowed_ips.description:
A new list of networks, replacing the old one, checked as at
creation.

200.description: The firewall as it now is.

409.description:
`firewall_exists`: its container has another live firewall with that
name.

delete.description:
Deletes a firewall that no live API token is held to. Deleting one from
under its keys would leave them usable from anywhere, so that is
`409 firewall_in_use`, which counts them: lift it from each with
`PATCH /v1/api-tokens/{id}` first. A revoked key does not count. Audited
as `delete_firewall`, a refusal included; another tenant's firewall, a
deleted one and an id never issued are the same 404, unaudited.

409.description: `firewall_in_use`: live API tokens are held to it.

get.summary: Read the tenant's billing standing and this month's estimate
get.description:
Where the tenant's billing stands, and what the current UTC month's
paid keys and overage come to so far. Everything here is read from
rypt's own database — the standing is what Stripe's webhook last
delivered, the estimate is computed from the tenant's keys and usage
— so reading it never waits on Stripe.

The estimate is before tax, and is only an estimate: the invoice Stripe
issues once the month has closed is the bill. In the month a
subscription starts, or starts again after one lapsed, the tenant's
paid keys are billed for every day of that month they existed, the days
before the subscription included — a whole key-month each, in a month
before October 2026 — as they are counted here; overage from before the
tenant's first subscription in the month is counted here too, but is
never billed; after a lapse within the month, the overage in between is
billed. Earlier months without a subscription are never billed.

From October 2026 a paid key's fee is counted for its days so far,
through today, so it grows by a day's share each day the key is kept,
and never for fewer days than have already been sent to Stripe. Its
allowance is its share for its days to the month's last, or to the day
its deletion was requested if it was, so the overage is what the
invoice will say if nothing changes. A key still pending deletion is
counted as if it will not be restored; Stripe is told so only once the
month has closed, since a restore would undo it, so until then the
overage here can be ahead of what has been sent.

In a month before October 2026, a paid key less than a day old is
counted, unless it was created on the month's last day, and drops out
if it is deleted before it is a day old. A key-month already sent to
Stripe is counted whatever the rules say of it now.

Not metered, not audited: reading billing changes nothing.

Exists only where the deployment configures billing. Elsewhere this
path is `404 not_found`, which is how a client tells that billing is
switched off rather than broken.

200.description: The tenant's standing and this month's estimate.

post.summary: Start a subscription on Stripe Checkout
post.description:
Creates a Stripe Checkout session for the tenant's subscription and
returns its URL, for the dashboard to send the browser to. The card,
billing address and tax id are entered on Stripe's page and never
pass through rypt. The first call also creates the tenant's Stripe
customer, and every later one reuses it — a lapsed tenant coming back
included. Two first calls at once make one customer between them:
the second, arriving while the first is still creating it, is
`503 unavailable`, and trying again gets that customer.

Stripe sends the browser back to the deployment's billing return URL
(`RYPT_BILLING_RETURN_URL`) — with `?checkout=done` appended once the
customer completes the page, unchanged if they turn back instead.
Coming back proves nothing by itself: the subscription reaches rypt
through Stripe's webhook, usually within seconds, so
`GET /v1/billing` can still say `none` for a moment after
`checkout=done`.

Each call makes a new session, whose URL Stripe keeps open for 24
hours; follow it at once rather than storing it. A tenant whose
subscription is still open — `active`, `past_due` while Stripe
retries a payment, or `unpaid` once the retries ran out — is
`409 billing_active`, because a second subscription would bill every
key twice; the portal is where it changes its card or pays the open
invoice.

Stripe not answering, answering with a 5xx or a 429, or answering
409 because another request is still creating the tenant's customer,
is `503 unavailable`: try again in a moment. Any other failure is
`500 internal_error` — among them a Stripe account the operator has
not yet prepared with `rypt-admin stripe setup`, which is found before
a customer is created, so nothing is left behind.

Takes no request body. Not audited: it changes nothing a key or a
credential depends on, and the subscription it leads to arrives by
webhook. Exists only where the deployment configures billing, and is
`404 not_found` elsewhere.

200.description: The Checkout page to send the browser to.

409.description:
`billing_active`: the tenant already has an open subscription
(`active`, `past_due` or `unpaid`), so there is nothing to set up.
Manage it, or pay its open invoice, through
`POST /v1/billing/portal`.

post.description:
Creates a Stripe customer portal session and returns its URL, for the
dashboard to send the browser to. Invoices, the payment method, the
billing address, the tax id and cancellation all live there, on
Stripe's page, rather than being rebuilt here. The portal's way back
leads to the deployment's billing return URL
(`RYPT_BILLING_RETURN_URL`).

Stripe expires the URL five minutes after it is made unless it is
used, so follow it at once. A cancellation made in the portal takes
effect at the end of the billing period; once Stripe's webhook has
delivered it, `GET /v1/billing` shows the date as `cancel_at`.

Open to a tenant in any standing that has a Stripe customer, a
lapsed one included: it may still have invoices to read or to pay. A
tenant that has never started a checkout has no Stripe customer and
nothing to manage: `409 billing_not_set_up`. Stripe failures are
`503` or `500` as for `POST /v1/billing/checkout`.

Takes no request body. Not audited, for the same reason as
`POST /v1/billing/checkout`. Exists only where the deployment
configures billing, and is `404 not_found` elsewhere.

200.description: The portal page to send the browser to.

409.description:
`billing_not_set_up`: the tenant has no Stripe customer yet. Set
billing up through `POST /v1/billing/checkout` first.

post.description:
Stripe calls this; clients never do. It is how rypt learns that a
subscription started, changed, fell behind on payment or ended — the
console endpoints never ask Stripe for the standing, so this is the
only way it changes.

It takes no credential. Each delivery is authenticated instead by its
`Stripe-Signature` header: an HMAC-SHA256, under the endpoint's
signing secret, of the timestamp and the exact bytes of the body. A
missing or non-matching signature, or a timestamp more than five
minutes old, is `400 invalid_request`, and nothing in the body is
acted on. So is a signed body that is not a JSON object, or an event
without the `id`, `type` and `data` every event has. A body over
128 KiB is `413 payload_too_large`, as on every route.

An event counts only through the subscription it names, which is
fetched afresh from Stripe, so events that arrive late, out of order
or twice all settle on Stripe's current state. A delivery that finds
the tenant's account changed by another while it was fetching applies
nothing and fetches again — what every checkout's pair of events at
once meets — and only an account that changes under it three times
running is `500`, so that Stripe redelivers it. An event already handled, one of a type rypt
does not act on, one for a customer rypt does not know, and a thin
notification rather than a snapshot event are all `200`, because a
retry could not change them. So is one naming a subscription Stripe
no longer has, in test mode; in live mode, where Stripe never deletes
a subscription, that means the deployment's secret key is for another
account or mode, and it is `500` so that Stripe retries until the key
is put right. A database or Stripe failure is `500`, which Stripe
retries.

Exists only where the deployment configures billing, and is
`404 not_found` elsewhere.

parameters.name: Stripe-Signature
parameters.description:
`t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC>`, with one `v1` per active
signing secret while a secret is being rolled; any match is
accepted.

schema.description:
A Stripe event, in the API version the endpoint was created
with. Deliberately unconstrained: Stripe's event shapes are
Stripe's to extend, and the signature, not this schema, is
what vouches for the body.

200.description: Received — acted on now or before, or not needed. No body.

400.description:
`invalid_request`. The `Stripe-Signature` header is missing,
malformed, too old or matches no signature, or a signed body is
not a JSON object or not an event.

500.description:
`internal_error`. Nothing was applied and the event is not
recorded, so Stripe delivers it again: a database or Stripe
failure, a failed cancellation of a subscription the event makes
redundant, the tenant's account changed by another delivery while
this one fetched the subscription, or — in live mode only — a
subscription Stripe does not have. The cause is logged and never
returned.

get.description:
No authentication, no database call, no KMS call: it answers whether
this process is up and serving.

The same handler as `/v1/healthz`. In the Cloud Run deployment Google's
frontend answers the root path itself, so a request here never reaches
the container; `/v1/healthz` is the one to probe in production.

bearerAuth.description:
`Authorization: Bearer ry_<prefix>_<secret>` — 44 characters: `ry_`, an
8-character prefix, `_`, a 32-character secret, all base62. Issued by
`rypt-admin apikey create` or by `POST /v1/api-tokens`, and shown once.

consoleAuth.description:
`Authorization: Bearer <Auth0 access token>` — an RS256 JWT issued by
the operator's Auth0 tenant for this API's audience. Used by the
dashboard; a browser cannot hold an API token.

Served only when the deployment configures a console. Where it is
offered alongside `bearerAuth`, either credential is accepted and both
resolve to the same tenant.

name.description: Unique among the tenant's live containers.

is_default.description:
The tenant's default container: there is exactly one, everything
goes in it unless told otherwise, and it cannot be deleted.

id.description: Used in `/v1/firewalls/{id}`, and as an API token's `firewall_id`.

container_id.description:
The container it lives in. Only that container's API tokens can be
held to it.

name.description: Unique among its container's live firewalls.

allowed_ips.description:
Networks in CIDR notation (an address alone is `/32` or `/128`),
ascending.

id.description: Key id, used in every `/v1/keys/{id}` path.

container_id.description: The container it lives in, fixed at creation.

name.description: Tenant-chosen name, unique among its container's live keys.

versions.description:
Short ids of the key's enabled versions, ascending: every version
that still decrypts, the retiring ones included.

primary_version.description:
Short id of the version new ciphertext is produced under. Always one
of `versions`, and never retiring.

retiring_versions.description:
The versions a rotation retired, ascending, each with the time it
is destroyed. Each is also in `versions`. Empty when none is
retiring.

state.description:
`active`, or `pending_deletion`: deleted, not yet destroyed, and
refusing every operation until it is restored.

delete_requested_at.description:
When deletion was requested, RFC 3339 in UTC, to microseconds.
Null unless the key is pending deletion.

destroy_after.description:
When a key pending deletion is destroyed, unless it is restored
first: seven days after `delete_requested_at`. From this time on
it can no longer be restored. The destruction happens at the
service's first sweep after it, so the key may still be listed as
pending for a while, longer when the service has been idle. Null
unless the key is pending deletion.

When the version is destroyed: seven days after the rotation that
retired it, RFC 3339 in UTC, to microseconds. Until then it
decrypts, unwraps and rewraps; from the service's first sweep after
it, it never will again. The sweep runs every few minutes, later
when the service has been idle, so the version may still be listed
for a while after this time.

ciphertext.description:
The ciphertext, base64. It names the key version it was made under,
so `decrypt` keeps working across rotations.

key_id.description:
Key the operation was on. Null on a failed `create_key`, whose row
was rolled back or never inserted.

api_token_id.description:
API token the request presented. Null for an operation performed
from the console, which presents an Auth0 access token instead.

user_id.description:
Console user the request authenticated as. Null for an operation
performed with an API token. Exactly one of this and `api_token_id`
is set on every event a request caused since the console existed;
both are null on older rows, on the `destroy_key` the service
records when it destroys a key whose pending deletion ran out, and
on the `destroy_version` it records when it destroys a version whose
seven days after a rotation ran out.

op.description:
Operation name. `rename_key` is a change of the key's name; the
event records neither name. `delete_key` is a deletion requested,
which puts the key in pending deletion; `restore_key` takes it out
again; and `destroy_key` is its destruction, by delete now or, with
no API token, user or address, by the service once the pending
deletion ran out. `destroy_version` is the destruction of one
version a rotation retired, by the service once its seven days ran
out, with no API key, user or address; `kms_version` names the
version. `create_api_token`, `update_api_token` and
`revoke_api_token`, and the container and firewall operations, are
recorded with no `key_id`, so this endpoint — which reads one key's
history — never returns them.

kms_version.description:
Short KMS version id the operation used. For `decrypt` and `unwrap`
it is the key's primary version if that is what the ciphertext
named, and null otherwise. For `destroy_version`, the version
destroyed.

error_code.description:
The error envelope's code, for a failed operation. A refused one
included: `action_not_allowed` for an action the API token was not
given, `key_not_allowed` for a key outside its `key_ids`.

request_id.description:
The `x-request-id` of the request that caused the event, or, for a
`destroy_key` or `destroy_version` the service recorded on its own,
an id it made for the occasion.

src_ip.description:
The address the request came from. Null only on a `destroy_key` or
`destroy_version` the service recorded on its own, which no request
caused.

bytes.description:
Size of the operation's input in bytes, never any content. Null
when the request failed before its input was decoded.

kms_us.description:
How long the key-management backend took, in microseconds: the one
call `encrypt`, `decrypt`, `wrap` and `unwrap` make, and both of
`rewrap`'s. Recorded for a call that failed too. Null for every
other operation, and for one refused before the backend was called.

id.description:
Stable id for this person, and what `audit_events.user_id`
records.

email.description:
The email the access token last carried, or null. Null on a
default Auth0 setup, which puts no profile in an access token.

created_at.description: When they first authenticated. RFC 3339 in UTC.

id.description: The tenant every other endpoint scopes this caller to.

name.description:
For a tenant created at first login, the user's own email, or
their Auth0 subject when the token carried no email.

role.description:
The role held in that tenant. Every user today owns the one tenant
they were provisioned with; nothing yet grants a second membership.

name.description:
The label it was created with. Null for a key made with
`rypt-admin`, which has no person to name it.

created_by_user_id.description: The console user who created it, if one did.

revoked_at.description: When it was revoked, or null while it is live.

container_id.description: The container it lives in and never sees outside of.

firewall_id.description: The firewall it is held to, or null for none.

key_ids.description:
Keys of its container it may act on, ascending; null for all of
them. A key destroyed since it was named stays in the list.

AllowedActions.description:
What an API token may do with the keys it may act on: `encrypt`,
`decrypt`, `wrap`, `unwrap`, `rewrap` and `rotate` use a key or rotate
it, `rename`, `delete` and `restore` change its lifecycle, and `create`
makes a new one in the key's container, for a key with no `key_ids`
alone. `read` is for listing keys, reading a key and its audit log,
and reading usage. Empty allows nothing. Repeats are dropped, and
the list is returned sorted. API tokens made before 0.8.0 were not
given the four lifecycle actions; those that existed when 0.14.0
was deployed were given `read`.

ChainHead.description: The latest entry of a container's permission chain.

seq.description: Its position; 0 is the chain's genesis entry.

hash.description:
Its SHA-256 hash, lowercase hex, which covers the hash of the entry
before it and so every entry back to genesis. The serialization is
specified in `crates/rypt-core/src/permissions.rs`.

container_id.description: The container whose chain this is.
The container it lives in and never sees outside of.

name.description: The label it was created with.

prefix.description:
The token's 8-character lookup prefix. Returned here and nowhere
else; it gives nothing away, because it is already inside `token`.

token.description:
**The plaintext API token, returned exactly once.** Not stored and
not recoverable: the database holds only its Argon2id hash.

container_id.description:
The container the key lives in, so the line of a destroyed key,
which no key listing carries any more, can still be placed.

ops.description:
Operations performed in the period, including any past the
allowance.

overage_ops.description:
How many of those operations were past the key's `allowance`. On a
paid tier this is the quantity overage is billed on: from October
2026, `ops` less `allowance`, never below 0; in a month before,
counted operation by operation against the cap in force when each
happened. On `free`, which refuses new ciphertext at the cap
rather than allowing overage, it counts the decrypts and unwraps
past the cap, and the few operations concurrent requests can carry
past it, none of which are ever billed.

cap.description:
The key tier's monthly cap: on `free` a hard limit on `encrypt`,
`wrap` and `rewrap`, past which `decrypt` and `unwrap` go on, and
on the paid tiers the included allowance of a key that exists all
month.
Always the tier's, whatever `allowance` says.

allowance.description:
The key's included operations for the period. It is `cap`, but for
a paid key in a month from October 2026, whose allowance is split
by the day like its fee: `cap × days / days in the month`, rounded
down. Its days are the UTC days it exists in, from the day it was
created, or the 1st, through the day its deletion was requested,
if it was, or the month's last, both counted; so a key that exists
for 10 days of a 30-day month includes 10/30 of `cap`. A month
that has ended is not reopened: a key still pending deletion when
it ended keeps, for that month, the share it was billed with, to
the day its deletion was requested, even if it has been restored
since.

status.description:
Where the tenant's subscription stands, as Stripe's webhook last
delivered it. `none` — no subscription yet: never subscribed, or a
checkout started and not completed. `active` — in good
standing (Stripe's `active` or `trialing`). `past_due` — a payment
failed and Stripe is retrying it; still good standing, so nothing
stops meanwhile, and the portal is where the card is fixed.
`unpaid` — Stripe's retries ran out and the subscription is still
open with an unpaid invoice: paying it in the portal
(`POST /v1/billing/portal`) restores good standing, and checkout
is `409 billing_active`, because a second subscription beside the
open one would bill every key twice. `lapsed` — anything else:
cancelled, paused or never completed; setting billing up again
through `POST /v1/billing/checkout` restores it. Under `unpaid`
and `lapsed`, paid keys still decrypt and unwrap, but `encrypt`,
`wrap`, `rewrap` and creating a paid key are
`402 billing_required`.

period.description: The UTC calendar month the estimate covers, always the current one.

cancel_at.description:
When the subscription is due to end, after a cancellation in the
portal; null when no end is scheduled. Until then it bills and
works as before. Also null once the tenant is no longer in good
standing: `status` already says the subscription is over, and a
date in the past would read as an end still to come.

BillingEstimate.description:
What the period's paid keys and their overage come to so far, before
tax. The invoice Stripe issues after the month closes is the bill,
with any tax added.

currency.description: ISO 4217 code, lower case, as Stripe writes it.

lines.description:
One line per paid tier — `wrapped`, `software`, `hsm`, in that
order — whether or not the tenant has a key on it, so a price
list can be drawn from the lines alone.

tier.description: A paid tier. `free` is never billed, so never listed.

key_months.description:
The tenant's keys on this tier billed for the period. From October
2026, every one billed at least one day of it so far. In a month
before, every one that existed at any point in it — its deletion,
if requested, not requested before the period began — except one
deleted within 24 hours of being created and not restored, and one
created on the period's last day; each is one key-month, billed in
full.

key_days.description:
The days those keys are billed for so far, summed. A key's days
are the UTC days it exists in, from the day it was created, or the
1st, through today or the day its deletion was requested,
whichever is earlier, both counted, and never fewer than have
already been sent to Stripe. In a month before October 2026 a
key-month counts every day of the month, so `key_days` is
`key_months × days_in_period`: in any month,
`key_days / days_in_period` is the key-months the fee is for.

days_in_period.description:
How many days the period's UTC month has, 28 to 31: what a paid
key's fee and allowance are split into from October 2026.

fee_cents.description:
The tier's fee per key-month — one key for a whole month — in
cents. From October 2026 a key pays its days over `days_in_period`
of it.

overage_ops.description:
Operations beyond the included allowance, summed across this
tier's keys for the period. From October 2026 each key's are its
operations past its `allowance`, as `GET /v1/usage` gives it: a
key still pending deletion is counted as if it will not be
restored, which Stripe is told only once the month has closed.

overage_millicents_per_op.description:
The tier's price per overage operation, in thousandths of a cent.
An integer because the price is a fraction of a cent.

fee_amount_cents.description:
What the keys' fees come to, in cents, rounded half up to the cent
on its own, as Stripe rounds the tier's key-months line of the
invoice. In a month before October 2026 it is
`key_months × fee_cents`. From then on it is `fee_cents` times the
keys' shares of a key-month, summed: each share is the key's days
over `days_in_period`, rounded to nine decimal places as Stripe is
sent it, so a key that exists all month pays exactly `fee_cents`,
and `key_days / days_in_period × fee_cents` is this to within a
cent.

overage_amount_cents.description:
What the overage comes to, in cents:
`overage_ops × overage_millicents_per_op / 1000`, rounded half up
to the cent on its own, as Stripe rounds the tier's overage line
of the invoice.

amount_cents.description:
What the line comes to: `fee_amount_cents` plus
`overage_amount_cents`. Each is rounded before they are added,
because Stripe rounds each invoice line, and a tier's fees are one
line and its overage another; so half a cent of each comes to two
cents, not one.

url.description:
A Stripe-hosted page to send the browser to. Short-lived, and
specific to this tenant: follow it at once, never store it.

Error.description:
Every error, from every layer, has this envelope. `cap` and `resets_at`
are present only on `ops_cap_reached`.

message.description:
Human-readable detail. Never names a GCP resource, a permission or
an internal cause.

request_id.description: The same value as the response's `x-request-id`.

resets_at.description:
Midnight UTC on the first of the next month, when the counter
resets. `ops_cap_reached` only.

Unauthorized.description:
`unauthorized`. A missing header, the wrong scheme, a malformed token,
an unknown prefix, a revoked key and a wrong secret are all
indistinguishable.

PaymentRequired.description:
`billing_required`. Only where the deployment configures billing,
and only while the tenant's billing is not in good standing: no
subscription, or one that is cancelled, unpaid, paused or never
completed. A payment Stripe is still retrying is good standing —
nothing stops while it tries again.

It answers creating a key on a paid tier (`wrapped`, `software`,
`hsm`), and `encrypt`, `wrap` and `rewrap` on a paid-tier key: the
operations that start a new charge or produce new ciphertext. It
also answers `rotate` on a paid-tier key, because a rotation retires
the old version and a lapsed tenant could not rewrap off it before
it is destroyed.
`decrypt` and `unwrap` are never refused for billing, so a lapsed
tenant can always recover its data, and a `free` key is unaffected.
Setting billing up again in the console clears it.

Forbidden.description:
The credential is valid but is the wrong kind for this endpoint:
`api_token_required` on an endpoint an API token must reach, or
`session_required` on one only a console session may. Also `no_tenant`,
for an authenticated user who belongs to no tenant; and, for an API
token its owner restricted, `ip_not_allowed` from outside its firewall's
networks — on any endpoint, naming the address — `key_not_allowed` for a
key outside its list, or a create, and `action_not_allowed` for
`encrypt`, `decrypt`, `wrap`, `unwrap`, `rewrap` or `rotate`, a rename,
a delete, a restore, a create or a read (listing keys, reading a key or
its audit log, reading usage) when it was not given that action. A
refused read is not recorded in the audit log.

NotFound.description:
`not_found`. An unknown route, or a key id that is unknown, destroyed,
not a UUID, another tenant's, or — for an API token — another
container's: the API never confirms that an id exists. A key pending deletion is still found: it is not `404`, and
it refuses operations with `409 key_pending_deletion`.

KeyPendingDeletion.description:
`key_pending_deletion`. The key is pending deletion: it refuses every
operation, `decrypt` and `unwrap` included, until it is restored with
`POST /v1/keys/{id}/restore`. The message says when it will be
destroyed. The refusal is audited, so the key's log shows what still
tried to use it, and it is never counted.

PayloadTooLarge.description:
`payload_too_large`. A body over 128 KiB, a `plaintext` over 65,536
bytes, an `aad` over 65,520 bytes on a `software` or `hsm` key (65,536
on a `free` or `wrapped` one), or an `hsm` key's `plaintext` (or
`dek`) + `aad` over 8,176 bytes.

TooManyRequests.description:
`ops_cap_reached` — `encrypt`, `wrap`, `rewrap` or `rotate` on a
`free` key at its monthly cap, carrying `cap` and `resets_at`;
`decrypt` and `unwrap` are never refused at the cap — or
`rate_limited`, over 100 requests per second for this API token.

InternalError.description:
`internal_error`. A database failure, a KMS failure other than a bad
ciphertext, a Stripe failure, or a panic. The cause is logged with the
request id and never returned.

Unavailable.description:
`unavailable`. A bounded internal queue was full for longer than its
wait, or — on `POST /v1/billing/checkout` and
`POST /v1/billing/portal` — Stripe did not answer, or answered with a
5xx or a 429, or — on checkout — a 409 because another checkout for
the tenant was still creating its customer, or — on the ten routes an
API token's actions govern — the policy decision point did not answer.
Nothing is wrong with the request; retry it.
